newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU grain export tender produces avalanche of bids.
newsitem.headline: EU grain export tender produces avalanche of bids.

text.p: Export fever in the world grain market spread to the European Union's weekly grain tender on Thursday as traders sought EU subsidies to sell more than a million tonnes of wheat.
A surge of imports from North Africa, Iraq's return to the world oil market to raise money for food and now hopes that Russia and India will start buying have pushed up demand.
French cereals office ONIC said trading firms had bid through France on Thursday for 1.32 million tonnes of soft wheat from the open market inside the European Union for export.
That was exactly twice the volume sought the previous week.
The bidding pulled Europe's internal grain market out of what to many traders looked like a pre-Christmas slumber.
"It's a surprise. Someone has done something," said one trader in France, where spot soft wheat prices rose five francs a tonne, or almost one percent, for delivery at Rouen.
Others mentioned speculation that Russia or Iraq -- about to load oil for the first time in six years -- were lining up important grain deals.
Import demand around North Africa and constant interest from Eastern Europe, hit by several bad crops this year, has also caught the market's attention, traders said.

Hopes for wheat to Russia, and talk that India would be importing wheat rather than exporting it for a while, provided bullish arguments in Chicago futures pits overnight. But traders on both sides of the Atlantic said doubts remained over both.
Any Indian purchases would benefit Australia, while Russia did not have the money to sponsor significant imports.
"It's not the mathematics of prices you want to see with Russia, it's the cash," a Geneva-based trader said.
Higher Argentine prices and delivery problems also boosted European demand, traders said.
Some firms were said to be re-pricing optional-origin wheat deals first drawn up on an Argentine basis in European terms.
Some traders said European wheat still looked expensive, however, and doubted that exporters already had business matching the EU wheat bids on their books.
"This has got to be a few people going long," said one.

The head of France's ONIC cereals office, Alain Moulinier, said he felt the bidding volume was normal set against the fact there would be a two-week gap without export tenders over Christmas and the New Year.
He doubted the bids were all to cover existing business.
The EU will hold an export tender next Thursday but not for the next two weeks after that.
